cor-outer-product-expansion.title: Outer Product Expansion
cor-outer-product-expansion.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) have columns a1,…,an∈Fm, and let B∈Mn×p(F) have rows r1,…,rn∈M1×p(F). Then AB=a1r1+a2r2+⋯+anrn=∑k=1nakrk, where each akrk∈Mm×p(F) is column k of A times row k of B.

cor-sherman-morrison.title: Sherman–Morrison Formula
cor-sherman-morrison.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be invertible and u,v∈Fn. Then A+uvT is invertible if and only if 1+vTA−1u≠0, and in that case (A+uvT)−1=A−1−A−1uvTA−11+vTA−1u. Moreover det(A+uvT)=detA(1+vTA−1u).

def-block-diagonal.title: Block Diagonal Matrix
def-block-diagonal.html: Let k1,…,kr be positive integers and Ai∈Mki(F) square for each i. Their direct sum A1⊕⋯⊕Ar is the matrix in Mk1+⋯+kr(F) which, with row partition and column partition both equal to k1,…,kr, has (i,i) block Ai and (i,j) block 0 for i≠j. A square matrix is block diagonal with respect to the partition k1,…,kr if it has this form. For two blocks, A⊕B=(A00B).

def-block-partition.title: Block Partition
def-block-partition.html:
Let A=(aij)∈Mm×n(F). A row partition of A is a list of positive integers m1,…,ma with m1+⋯+ma=m, and a column partition is a list of positive integers n1,…,nb with n1+⋯+nb=n. Put μr=m1+⋯+mr and νs=n1+⋯+ns, with μ0=ν0=0. For 1≤r≤a and 1≤s≤b, the (r,s) block of A is the matrix Ars∈Mmr×ns(F) with entries (Ars)ij=aμr−1+i, νs−1+j(1≤i≤mr, 1≤j≤ns). We then write A=(Ars), displayed as an a×b array of blocks, and call A a block matrix.

Let B∈Mn×p(F). Partitions of A and B are conformable if the column partition of A and the row partition of B are the same list n1,…,nb, in the same order.

def-commutator.title: Commutator
def-commutator.html: Let n≥1 and A,B∈Mn(F). The commutator of A and B is [A,B]:=AB−BA∈Mn(F). A matrix C∈Mn(F) is a commutator if C=[X,Y] for some X,Y∈Mn(F). For operators S,T∈L(V) on a vector space V, we write likewise [S,T]:=ST−TS∈L(V).

def-kronecker-product.title: Kronecker product
def-kronecker-product.html: Let A=(aij)∈Mm×n(F) and B=(bkl)∈Mp×q(F), of any sizes. The Kronecker product of A and B is the mp×nq block matrix A⊗B:=(a11Ba12B⋯a1nBa21Ba22B⋯a2nB⋮⋮⋮am1Bam2B⋯amnB)∈Mmp×nq(F), with m rows and n columns of blocks, each block of size p×q (@def-block-partition).

def-schur-complement.title: Schur Complement
def-schur-complement.html:
Let M=(ABCD)∈M(k+p)×(k+l)(F) be a block matrix with A∈Mk(F), B∈Mk×l(F), C∈Mp×k(F) and D∈Mp×l(F), where k,p,l≥1.

  1. If A is invertible, the Schur complement of A in M is M/A:=D−CA−1B∈Mp×l(F).
  2. Symmetrically, if M=(ABCD) with D∈Ml(F) invertible, A∈Mm×k(F), B∈Mm×l(F) and C∈Ml×k(F), the Schur complement of D in M is M/D:=A−BD−1C∈Mm×k(F).

def-vec-operator.title: Vectorization
def-vec-operator.html: Let X=(xij)∈Mm×n(F) have columns x1,…,xn∈Fm. Its vectorization is the column vector vecX:=(x1x2⋮xn)∈Fmn, whose entry in position (j−1)m+i is xij, for 1≤i≤m, 1≤j≤n.

exm-block-inverse-4x4.title: A 4 \times 4 Inverse through a 2 \times 2 Schur Complement
exm-block-inverse-4x4.title_html: A 4×4 Inverse through a 2×2 Schur Complement
exm-block-inverse-4x4.html: Invert M=(110−112−1−1−1−111010−1)∈M4(Q) using @thm-block-inverse-formula, and find detM.

exm-commutator-3x3.title: Writing a Trace-Zero 3 \times 3 Matrix as a Commutator
exm-commutator-3x3.title_html: Writing a Trace-Zero 3×3 Matrix as a Commutator
exm-commutator-3x3.html: Over Q, write A=(12001110−2) as a commutator [X,Y].

exm-cyclic-shift-block-triangular.title: A Plane Mapped into Itself
exm-cyclic-shift-block-triangular.html: Let T:R3→R3, T(x,y,z)=(y,z,x), and U={(x,y,z):x+y+z=0}. Show that T maps U into U, find [T]B for the basis B=(u1,u2,e3) with u1=(1,−1,0), u2=(0,1,−1), and interpret the lower-right block.

exm-heisenberg-characteristic-p.title: The Identity as a Commutator in Characteristic p
exm-heisenberg-characteristic-p.title_html: The Identity as a Commutator in Characteristic p
exm-heisenberg-characteristic-p.html: Let F have prime characteristic p (for instance F=Fp). Let Dp∈Mp(F) have (k,k+1)-entry k⋅1 for 1≤k≤p−1, and let Sp∈Mp(F) have (k+1,k)-entry 1 for 1≤k≤p−1, all other entries 0. Show that [Dp,Sp]=Ip.

exm-rank-i-minus-ab.title: Rank of I - AB versus I - BA
exm-rank-i-minus-ab.title_html: Rank of I−AB versus I−BA
exm-rank-i-minus-ab.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×m(F).

  1. Prove that rank(Im−AB)+n=rank(In−BA)+m.
  2. Deduce that for m=n, rank(In−AB)=rank(In−BA), and In−AB is invertible if and only if In−BA is.
  3. Check (a) for A=(110011) and B=(100001) over Q.

exm-sylvester-equation-vec.title: A Sylvester Equation as a Linear System
exm-sylvester-equation-vec.title_html: A Sylvester Equation as a Linear System
exm-sylvester-equation-vec.html: Solve AX+XB=C over Q, where A=(1102),B=(1011),C=(1−113).

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: A1
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html:
1. Define the Schur complement M/A, including the hypothesis on A and the size of M/A.
  2. State the block LDU factorization of M in terms of A and M/A.
  3. True or false: if M=(ABCD) is invertible and A is square, then A is invertible. Justify your answer.
  4. If A is invertible and M is invertible, which block of M−1 is (M/A)−1?
  5. True or false: for all A,B,C,D∈Mn(F) with CD=DC, det(ABCD)=det(AD−BC), even if D is not invertible and F=F2. Justify your answer.

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: B1: A Schur complement, a determinant and a rank
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title_html: B1: A Schur complement, a determinant and a rank
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html: Let M=(2110113112950164)∈M4(Q). Compute M/A for the upper-left block A. Hence find detM and rankM, and decide whether M is invertible.

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: B2: A rank-one update
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html: Let A=diag(1,2,4)∈M3(Q), u=(1,1,1) and v=(1,−1,2). Use @cor-sherman-morrison to find det(A+uvT) and (A+uvT)−1, and check one entry.

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: B3: Identity corners
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html:
Let B∈Mk×l(F), C∈Ml×k(F) and M=(IkBCIl).

  1. Show that M is invertible if and only if S=Il−CB is, and write down M−1 in terms of S−1.
  2. Deduce the inverse of (IkB0Il).
  3. For B=(12) and C=(11) over Q, compute M−1.

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: C1: Sylvester’s determinant identity
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×m(F) with m,n≥1.

  1. Compute both Schur complements of the identity blocks in M=(Im−ABIn), and deduce det(Im+AB)=det(In+BA).
  2. Deduce that for every non-zero c∈F, det(cIm−AB)=cm−ndet(cIn−BA).
  3. Deduce @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma from (a).

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: C2: Pivots as Schur complements
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html:
Let A∈Mn(F), and for 1≤k≤n let Ak be its leading principal submatrix (the top-left k×k corner), as in @exr-lu-factorization-c1.

  1. Suppose Ak−1 is invertible, where 2≤k≤n, and write Ak=(Ak−1bcTd). Show that sk:=Ak/Ak−1 is the scalar d−cTAk−1−1b, and that detAk=detAk−1⋅sk.
  2. Suppose A1,…,An are all invertible, and put s1=a11. Prove that detAk=s1s2⋯sk for every k, and that every sk is non-zero.
  3. Keep the hypothesis of (b). In the proof of @exr-lu-factorization-c1 (c), the last pivot is z=d−xTy with y=L′−1b and xT=cTU′−1. Show that z=An/An−1. Deduce that the diagonal entries of U in the LU factorization are ukk=detAk/detAk−1, with detA0:=1.
  4. Check (c) for A=(211433879) over Q.

exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title: C3: When A and C commute
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.title_html: C3: When A and C commute
exr-block-determinants-and-schur-complem.html:
Let n≥1 and A,B,C,D∈Mn(F) with AC=CA, and M=(ABCD).

  1. Assume A is invertible. Use @thm-schur-determinant to prove detM=det(AD−CB).
  2. Remove the assumption that A is invertible, over any field, by adapting the proof of @thm-det-commuting-blocks with Ax=A+xIn.
  3. For A=I2, B=E12, C=E21, D=E11 in M2(Q), check that AC=CA, and compare detM, det(AD−CB) and det(AD−BC).

Hint for (b): multiply Mx on the left by a block matrix that clears the lower-left block.

exr-block-multiplication-a1.title: A1
exr-block-multiplication-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for partitions of A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×p(F) to be conformable.
  2. State the block multiplication formula for (ABCD)(A′B′C′D′).
  3. True or false: the top-left block of that product is A′A+C′B. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A∈Mk(F) and B∈Ml(F), then A⊕B=B⊕A. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if M=(AB0D) with A, D square is invertible, then M−1 is block upper triangular. Justify your answer.
  6. In a basis whose first k vectors form a basis of U, what does a zero lower-left block of [T]B say about T?

exr-block-multiplication-b1.title: B1: Multiplying block matrices
exr-block-multiplication-b1.html:
Let M=(12101−1203),N=(1001121−11)∈M3(Q), both with row and column partition 2,1.

  1. Compute MN blockwise, and check one block against the entry formula.
  2. Explain why the partitions would not be conformable if N were given the row partition 1,2 instead.

exr-block-multiplication-b2.title: B2: Inverting a block triangular matrix
exr-block-multiplication-b2.title_html: B2: Inverting a block triangular matrix
exr-block-multiplication-b2.html: Use @thm-block-triangular-inverse to find the inverse of M=(2110112100120001)∈M4(Q), and check one block of MM−1.

exr-block-multiplication-b3.title: B3: A projection in an adapted basis
exr-block-multiplication-b3.title_html: B3: A projection in an adapted basis
exr-block-multiplication-b3.html:
Let P=(01−1010001)∈M3(R), U=span((1,1,0),(0,1,1)) and W=span(e1).

  1. Show that P2=P, that Pu=u for u∈U and Pe1=0, and that R3=U⊕W.
  2. Let B=((1,1,0),(0,1,1),e1). Use @thm-direct-sum-block-diagonal to write down [TP]B without computing, and confirm it as S−1PS, where S has the vectors of B as columns.
  3. Hence find P100 and trP.

exr-block-multiplication-c1.title: C1: Square-zero matrices of half rank
exr-block-multiplication-c1.title_html: C1: Square-zero matrices of half rank
exr-block-multiplication-c1.html:
Let n≥1.

  1. For X∈Mn(F), let NX=(0X00)∈M2n(F). Show that NX2=0 and that rankNX=rankX.
  2. Let V have dimension 2n, and let T∈L(V) satisfy T2=0 and rankT=n. Show that imT=kerT. Choose w1,…,wn with (Tw1,…,Twn) a basis of imT, and put ui=Twi. Prove that B=(u1,…,un,w1,…,wn) is a basis of V and that [T]B=NIn.
  3. Deduce that for every invertible X∈Mn(F), the matrix NX is similar to NIn.

Hint: for the independence in (b), apply T.

exr-block-multiplication-c2.title: C2: Powers of block triangular matrices
exr-block-multiplication-c2.title_html: C2: Powers of block triangular matrices
exr-block-multiplication-c2.html:
Let A∈Mk(F), D∈Ml(F) and B∈Mk×l(F), and let M=(AB0D).

  1. Prove that for every j≥1, Mj=(AjSj0Dj),Sj=∑i=0j−1AiBDj−1−i.
  2. Deduce that if D=0, then Mj=(AjAj−1B00) for j≥1, and that if moreover Ar=0, then Mr+1=0.
  3. For A=(0100), B=(11) and D=(0), find the least j with Mj=0.

exr-commutators-and-shoda-a1.title: A1
exr-commutators-and-shoda-a1.html:
1. Define the commutator [A,B], and state what it means for a matrix to be a commutator.
  2. State Shoda’s theorem, including the hypothesis on the field.
  3. True or false: [A,B]=[B,A] for all A,B∈Mn(F). Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: over every field, every trace-zero matrix is similar to a matrix with zero diagonal. Justify your answer.
  5. Name the two places where the proof of Shoda’s theorem uses characteristic 0.
  6. Explain why @thm-span-of-commutators does not by itself prove Shoda’s theorem.

exr-commutators-and-shoda-b1.title: B1: A 2 \times 2 commutator
exr-commutators-and-shoda-b1.title_html: B1: A 2×2 commutator
exr-commutators-and-shoda-b1.html:
Over Q, let A=(3−21−3).

  1. Using v=e1 as in @lem-nonscalar-similar-zero-diagonal-entry, find an invertible P such that Z=P−1AP has zero diagonal.
  2. With X0=diag(0,1), find Y0 with [X0,Y0]=Z.
  3. Hence write A=[X,Y], and check your answer by multiplying out.

exr-commutators-and-shoda-b2.title: B2: A commutator over \nF_2
exr-commutators-and-shoda-b2.title_html: B2: A commutator over F2
exr-commutators-and-shoda-b2.html:
Work over F2, and let A=(1101).

  1. Show that trA=0 and that A is not scalar.
  2. Explain why v=e1 cannot be used in @lem-nonscalar-similar-zero-diagonal-entry, and use v=e2 instead to find P with P−1AP of zero diagonal.
  3. The field F2 has exactly two elements. Use them as the diagonal of X0 to write A as a commutator, by hand.
  4. Explain why the same method cannot write I2∈M2(F2) as a commutator, and recall a pair X,Y that does.

exr-commutators-and-shoda-b3.title: B3: Commuting with a diagonal matrix
exr-commutators-and-shoda-b3.title_html: B3: Commuting with a diagonal matrix
exr-commutators-and-shoda-b3.html:
Let F be any field, let d1,…,dn∈F be distinct, let D=diag(d1,…,dn), and define L:Mn(F)→Mn(F) by L(X)=[D,X].

  1. Show that L is linear.
  2. Prove that kerL is the set of diagonal matrices and imL is the set of matrices with zero diagonal.
  3. Check that your answer to (b) agrees with the Rank–Nullity Theorem.
  4. Hence decide whether (012304560)∈M3(Q) is a commutator with X=diag(1,2,3), and if so find Y.

exr-commutators-and-shoda-c1.title: C1: Trace-like functionals, again
exr-commutators-and-shoda-c1.html:
Let F be any field, n≥1, and let φ:Mn(F)→F be linear with φ(AB)=φ(BA) for all A,B∈Mn(F).

  1. Prove that φ vanishes on every trace-zero matrix.
  2. Deduce that φ=ctr, where c=φ(E11).
  3. Suppose F has characteristic 0 and, in addition, φ(In)=n⋅1. Deduce that φ=tr.
  4. Show that the conclusion of (c) fails over Fp when n=p.

Hint: for (a), use @thm-span-of-commutators.

exr-commutators-and-shoda-c2.title: C2: When A commutes with [A, B]
exr-commutators-and-shoda-c2.title_html: C2: When A commutes with [A,B]
exr-commutators-and-shoda-c2.html:
Let F be a field of characteristic 0, let A,B∈Mn(F), put C=[A,B], and suppose that AC=CA. The goal is to prove that C is nilpotent, that is, Cs=0 for some s≥1.

  1. Prove that Ck=[A,BCk−1] for every k≥1. Deduce that trCk=0 for every k≥1.
  2. Show that there are an integer s≥1 and g∈F[x] with g(0)≠0 such that Csg(C)=0.
  3. Let U=col(Cs) and r=dim⁡U, and suppose r≥1. Extend a basis of U to a basis of Fn, and let P be the matrix with these columns. Show that P−1CP=(D∗0N),D∈Mr(F), with Ns=0 and g(D)=0.
  4. Write g=g0+xh with g0=g(0)≠0. Show that Ir is a linear combination of Ds,Ds+1,…,Dd for some d≥s, and use (a) to reach a contradiction.
  5. Conclude that Cs=0.

Hint: in (c), compare the columns of P−1CkP for k=1 and k=s with the coordinates of vectors of U; in (d), take traces.

exr-kronecker-product-a1.title: A1
exr-kronecker-product-a1.html:
1. Define A⊗B for A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mp×q(F), and state its size.
  2. True or false: for all A,B∈M2(F), A⊗B=B⊗A. Justify your answer.
  3. State the mixed product rule, including the conditions on the sizes.
  4. True or false: det(A⊗B)=detAdetB for all A,B∈M2(R). Justify your answer.
  5. State the vec identity, and name the matrix M with vec(XB)=MvecX for X∈Mm×n(F), B∈Mn(F).

exr-kronecker-product-b1.title: B1: Computing with Kronecker products
exr-kronecker-product-b1.html:
Let A=(201−1) and B=(1103) over Q.

  1. Write out A⊗B and B⊗A.
  2. Compute tr, det and rank of A⊗B from @thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det, and check the trace directly.
  3. Compute A2⊗B2 and use it to write down (A⊗B)2 without multiplying 4×4 matrices. Justify the step.
  4. Hence find (A⊗B)−1.

exr-kronecker-product-b2.title: B2: One-sided equations
exr-kronecker-product-b2.html:
Let A∈Mm(F) and C∈Mm×n(F), and consider AX=C for X∈Mm×n(F).

  1. Write the equation in the form MvecX=vecC, and describe M as a block matrix.
  2. Explain why the system splits into n separate systems, one for each column of X.
  3. Hence show that AX=C has exactly one solution for every C if and only if A is invertible.
  4. Solve XA=C over Q by the same method, where A=(1213) and C=(3701).

exr-kronecker-product-b3.title: B3: Which identities hold?
exr-kronecker-product-b3.html:
Determine which of the following statements hold for all A,B,C∈M2(R). Justify your answer.

  1. (A⊗B)(A⊗B)=A2⊗B2.
  2. (A+B)⊗C=A⊗C+B⊗C.
  3. (A⊗B)T=BT⊗AT.
  4. A⊗B=0 implies A=0 or B=0.
  5. tr(A⊗B)=tr(B⊗A).
  6. A⊗B+B⊗A=2(A⊗B).

exr-kronecker-product-c1.title: C1: When is a Kronecker product invertible?
exr-kronecker-product-c1.title_html: C1: When is a Kronecker product invertible?
exr-kronecker-product-c1.html:
1. Let A∈Mn(F) and B∈Mm(F). Prove that A⊗B is invertible if and only if both A and B are invertible.
  2. Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mp×q(F) with mp=nq, so that A⊗B is square. Prove that if m≠n, then A⊗B is not invertible.
  3. Give an example of a 2×1 matrix A and a 1×2 matrix B for which A⊗B is a non-zero 2×2 matrix, and compute its rank.

exr-kronecker-product-c2.title: C2: Kronecker sums
exr-kronecker-product-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) and B∈Mm(F), and put K:=A⊗Im+In⊗B∈Mnm(F).

  1. Prove that (A⊗Im)(In⊗B)=(In⊗B)(A⊗Im), and deduce that K2=A2⊗Im+2(A⊗B)+In⊗B2.
  2. Show that for X∈Mm×n(F), vec(BX+XAT)=KvecX.
  3. Suppose A and B are upper triangular. Prove that K is upper triangular with diagonal entries aii+bkk, and deduce that BX+XAT=C has exactly one solution for every C∈Mm×n(F) if and only if aii+bkk≠0 for all i,k.
  4. For A=(120−1) and B=(1003) over Q, decide whether BX+XAT=C is solvable for every C. If not, find a C with no solution.

exr-rank-of-block-matrices-a1.title: A1
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-a1.html:
1. State the three inequalities of @thm-block-rank-inequalities.
  2. True or false: rank(AB0D)=rankA+rankD for all blocks of compatible sizes. Justify your answer.
  3. Which matrix do you multiply (ABCD) by, and on which side, to replace C by C−XA?
  4. True or false: rank(AB)=rankA+rankB whenever A and B have the same number of rows. Justify your answer.
  5. State Frobenius’s inequality, and explain how Sylvester’s inequality follows from it.

exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b1.title: B1: Ranks of block matrices
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b1.html:
Let A=(1224) and D=(1101) in M2(Q). Find the rank of each 4×4 matrix, citing the result you use. In which case is the lower bound of @thm-block-rank-inequalities (c) strict?

  1. M1=(A00D).
  2. M2=(AB0D) with B=(1326).
  3. M3=(AI200).

exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b2.title: B2: Shifted products
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b2.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F), B∈Mn×m(F) and c∈F with c≠0.

  1. By adapting @exm-rank-i-minus-ab, prove that rank(cIm−AB)+n=rank(cIn−BA)+m.
  2. Check (a) over Q for c=2, A=(110110) and B=(101010).
  3. Show by an example with m=1, n=2 that (a) can fail for c=0.

exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b3.title: B3: Idempotents by blocks
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b3.html:
Let A∈Mn(F).

  1. Starting from (A00In−A), use block elimination to prove rankA+rank(In−A)=n+rank(A−A2).
  2. Deduce that A2=A if and only if rankA+rank(In−A)=n.
  3. Compare (b) with what Chapter 3 says about projections.

Hint: first add block row 1 to block row 2, then add block column 2 to block column 1.

exr-rank-of-block-matrices-c1.title: C1: The rank of A - ABA
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-c1.title_html: C1: The rank of A−ABA
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×m(F).

  1. Verify, by block multiplication, the following chain, in which each arrow is multiplication by an invertible block triangular matrix: (A00In−BA)→(AA0In−BA)→(AABAIn)→(A−ABAA0In)→(A−ABA00In). Name each multiplier and the side it acts on.
  2. Deduce that rank(A−ABA)=rankA+rank(In−BA)−n.
  3. Suppose ABA=A. Show that BA is idempotent and that rank(BA)=rankA.

Hint for (c): use (b), then @exr-rank-of-block-matrices-b3.

exr-rank-of-block-matrices-c2.title: C2: Involutions and the field
exr-rank-of-block-matrices-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F).

  1. Suppose the characteristic of F is not 2. Starting from (A−In00A+In), prove that rank(A−In)+rank(A+In)=n+rank(A2−In).
  2. Deduce that if A2=In (and charF≠2), then rank(A−In)+rank(A+In)=n.
  3. Show that (b) fails over F2, and point to the step of (a) that breaks.

Hint for (a): add block column 2 to block column 1, and subtract block row 2 from block row 1; then −2In is an invertible pivot.

lem-evaluate-polynomial-matrix.title: Evaluating a Matrix of Polynomials
lem-evaluate-polynomial-matrix.html: Let c∈F, and let N,N′ be matrices with entries in F[x] of sizes for which the operations below are defined. Then (N+N′)(c)=N(c)+N′(c), (NN′)(c)=N(c)N′(c), and, for square N, (detN)(c)=det(N(c)).

lem-nonscalar-similar-zero-diagonal-entr.title: A Non-Scalar Matrix Has a Similar Matrix with Zero Corner
lem-nonscalar-similar-zero-diagonal-entr.title_html: A Non-Scalar Matrix Has a Similar Matrix with Zero Corner
lem-nonscalar-similar-zero-diagonal-entr.html: Let F be any field, let n≥2, and let A∈Mn(F) be not scalar. Then there is an invertible P∈Mn(F) such that the first column of P−1AP is e2. In particular P−1AP=(0rTe1A1) for some r∈Fn−1 and A1∈Mn−1(F) with trA1=trA, where e1∈Fn−1.

lem-trace-zero-similar-zero-diagonal.title: Trace Zero Means Similar to Zero Diagonal
lem-trace-zero-similar-zero-diagonal.title_html: Trace Zero Means Similar to Zero Diagonal
lem-trace-zero-similar-zero-diagonal.html: Let F be a field of characteristic 0, let n≥1, and let A∈Mn(F) with trA=0. Then A is similar to a matrix all of whose diagonal entries are 0.

prp-block-transpose.title: Transpose of a Block Matrix
prp-block-transpose.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) have row partition m1,…,ma, column partition n1,…,nb and blocks Ars. Give AT the row partition n1,…,nb and the column partition m1,…,ma. Then (AT)sr=(Ars)T. In particular (ABCD)T=(ATCTBTDT).

prp-commutator-properties.title: Rules for Commutators
prp-commutator-properties.html:
Let A,A′,B∈Mn(F), c∈F, and let P∈Mn(F) be invertible. Then:

  1. [A+A′,B]=[A,B]+[A′,B], [cA,B]=c[A,B], and [B,A]=−[A,B]; in particular the commutator is linear in each slot.
  2. P−1[A,B]P=[P−1AP,P−1BP].
  3. tr[A,B]=0.

prp-kronecker-swap-similar.title: Swapping the Factors Is a Permutation Similarity
prp-kronecker-swap-similar.title_html: Swapping the Factors Is a Permutation Similarity
prp-kronecker-swap-similar.html: Let n,m≥1. There is a permutation matrix P∈Mnm(F), depending only on n and m, such that B⊗A=P−1(A⊗B)Pfor all A∈Mn(F), B∈Mm(F). In particular A⊗B∼B⊗A, and Im⊗A=P−1(A⊗Im)P.

thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic.title: Arithmetic of Block Diagonal Matrices
thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic.html:
Let A,A′∈Mk(F), B,B′∈Ml(F) and c∈F. Then:

  1. (A⊕B)+(A′⊕B′)=(A+A′)⊕(B+B′), c(A⊕B)=cA⊕cB, and (A⊕B)(A′⊕B′)=AA′⊕BB′;
  2. (A⊕B)j=Aj⊕Bj for every j∈N, and p(A⊕B)=p(A)⊕p(B) for every p∈F[x];
  3. A⊕B is invertible if and only if A and B are both invertible, and then (A⊕B)−1=A−1⊕B−1;
  4. det(A⊕B)=detAdetB and tr(A⊕B)=trA+trB.

thm-block-elimination-rank.title: Block Elimination Preserves Rank
thm-block-elimination-rank.html:
Let M=(ABCD) be as above.

  1. For all X∈Mm×p(F), X′∈Mp×m(F), Y∈Mk×l(F) and Y′∈Ml×k(F), the matrices (ImX0Ip),(Im0X′Ip),(IkY0Il),(Ik0Y′Il) are invertible, and so are the block swaps (0IpIm0)∈Mm+p(F) and (0IkIl0)∈Mk+l(F). Hence multiplying M on the left or right by any product of such matrices does not change its rank. The swaps give (0IpIm0)M=(CDAB) and M(0IkIl0)=(BADC).
  2. If col(B)⊆col(A), or if row(B)⊆row(D), then rank(AB0D)=rankA+rankD.

thm-block-inverse-formula.title: Block Inverse Formula
thm-block-inverse-formula.html:
Let M=(ABCD)∈Mk+l(F) with A∈Mk(F) and D∈Ml(F).

  1. Suppose A is invertible, and let S=M/A. Then M is invertible if and only if S is invertible, and in that case M−1=(A−1+A−1BS−1CA−1−A−1BS−1−S−1CA−1S−1). In particular the lower-right l×l block of M−1 is (M/A)−1.
  2. Suppose D is invertible, and let S′=M/D. Then M is invertible if and only if S′ is invertible, and in that case M−1=(S′−1−S′−1BD−1−D−1CS′−1D−1+D−1CS′−1BD−1). In particular the upper-left k×k block of M−1 is (M/D)−1.

thm-block-ldu.title: Block LDU Factorization
thm-block-ldu.html:
Let M=(ABCD) be partitioned as in @def-schur-complement.

  1. If A∈Mk(F) is invertible, then M=(Ik0CA−1Ip)(A00M/A)(IkA−1B0Il).
  2. If D∈Ml(F) is invertible, then M=(ImBD−10Il)(M/D00D)(Ik0D−1CIl).

thm-block-multiplication.title: Block Multiplication
thm-block-multiplication.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×p(F) be conformably partitioned: A with row partition m1,…,ma and column partition n1,…,nb, and B with row partition n1,…,nb and column partition p1,…,pc. Partition AB∈Mm×p(F) with row partition m1,…,ma and column partition p1,…,pc. Then for all 1≤r≤a and 1≤t≤c, (AB)rt=∑s=1bArsBst=Ar1B1t+Ar2B2t+⋯+ArbBbt. Each product ArsBst is defined and lies in Mmr×pt(F).

thm-block-rank-inequalities.title: Rank Inequalities for Block Matrices
thm-block-rank-inequalities.html:
Let A∈Mm×k(F), B∈Mm×l(F), C∈Mp×k(F) and D∈Mp×l(F).

  1. max(rankA,rankB)≤rank(AB)≤rankA+rankB, and likewise max(rankA,rankC)≤rank(AC)≤rankA+rankC.
  2. rank(A00D)=rankA+rankD.
  3. rank(AB0D)≥rankA+rankD and rank(A0CD)≥rankA+rankD.

thm-block-triangular-inverse.title: Block Triangular Products and Inverses
thm-block-triangular-inverse.html:
Let k,l≥1, and let M=(AB0D) and M′=(A′B′0D′), with A,A′∈Mk(F), D,D′∈Ml(F) and B,B′∈Mk×l(F).

  1. MM′=(AA′AB′+BD′0DD′); in particular it is block upper triangular.
  2. M is invertible if and only if A and D are both invertible.
  3. In that case M−1=(A−1−A−1BD−10D−1).

thm-det-commuting-blocks.title: Determinant with Commuting Blocks
thm-det-commuting-blocks.html: Let n≥1 and A,B,C,D∈Mn(F) over any field F. If CD=DC, then det(ABCD)=det(AD−BC).

thm-direct-sum-block-diagonal.title: Direct Sums Give Block Diagonal Matrices
thm-direct-sum-block-diagonal.title_html: Direct Sums Give Block Diagonal Matrices
thm-direct-sum-block-diagonal.html:
Let V=U⊕W be finite-dimensional with U≠{0}≠W, let BU=(u1,…,uk) and BW=(w1,…,wl) be bases of U and W, and let B=(u1,…,uk,w1,…,wl). For T∈L(V), the following are equivalent:

  1. T maps U into U and W into W;
  2. [T]B is block diagonal with respect to the partition k,l.

In that case [T]B=[T|U]BU⊕[T|W]BW.

thm-frobenius-rank-block-proof.title: Frobenius’s Rank Inequality
thm-frobenius-rank-block-proof.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F), B∈Mn×p(F) and C∈Mp×q(F). Then rank(ABC)+rankB≥rank(AB)+rank(BC).

thm-invariant-subspace-block-triangular.title: Subspaces Mapped into Themselves Give Block Triangular Matrices
thm-invariant-subspace-block-triangular.title_html: Subspaces Mapped into Themselves Give Block Triangular Matrices
thm-invariant-subspace-block-triangular.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V), and U a subspace with {0}≠U≠V. Let BU=(u1,…,uk) be a basis of U, extended to a basis B=(u1,…,uk,w1,…,wl) of V.

  1. T maps U into U if and only if the lower-left l×k block of [T]B is zero.
  2. In that case the rule T¯(v+U)=Tv+U defines an operator T¯ on V/U, and [T]B=([T|U]BUB0[T¯]B¯) for some B∈Mk×l(F), where B¯=(w1+U,…,wl+U) is a basis of V/U.

thm-kronecker-properties.title: Properties of the Kronecker Product
thm-kronecker-properties.html:
Let c∈F. Whenever the sizes make each side defined:

  1. (Bilinearity) (A+A′)⊗B=A⊗B+A′⊗B, A⊗(B+B′)=A⊗B+A⊗B′, and (cA)⊗B=c(A⊗B)=A⊗(cB).
  2. (Associativity) (A⊗B)⊗C=A⊗(B⊗C) for all A∈Mm×n(F), B∈Mp×q(F), C∈Mr×s(F).
  3. (Mixed product rule) For A∈Mm×n(F), C∈Mn×t(F), B∈Mp×q(F) and D∈Mq×u(F), (A⊗B)(C⊗D)=(AC)⊗(BD).
  4. (Transpose) (A⊗B)T=AT⊗BT.
  5. (Inverse) If A∈Mn(F) and B∈Mm(F) are invertible, then A⊗B is invertible and (A⊗B)−1=A−1⊗B−1.

thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det.title: Rank, Trace and Determinant of a Kronecker Product
thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det.title_html: Rank, Trace and Determinant of a Kronecker Product
thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det.html:
1. For A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mp×q(F), rank(A⊗B)=rankA⋅rankB.
  2. For A∈Mn(F) and B∈Mm(F), tr(A⊗B)=trA⋅trB.
  3. For A∈Mn(F) and B∈Mm(F), det(A⊗B)=(detA)m(detB)n.

thm-schur-determinant.title: Schur Determinant Formula
thm-schur-determinant.html:
Let M=(ABCD)∈Mk+l(F) with A∈Mk(F), D∈Ml(F) and k,l≥1.

  1. If A is invertible, then detM=detA⋅det(M/A).
  2. If D is invertible, then detM=detD⋅det(M/D).

thm-schur-rank.title: Schur Rank Formula
thm-schur-rank.html: Let M=(ABCD) be partitioned as in @def-schur-complement. If A∈Mk(F) is invertible, then rankM=k+rank(M/A). Symmetrically, if D∈Ml(F) is invertible, then rankM=l+rank(M/D).

thm-shoda.title: Shoda’s Theorem
thm-shoda.html: Let F be a field of characteristic 0, let n≥1, and let A∈Mn(F). Then A is a commutator, that is A=[X,Y] for some X,Y∈Mn(F), if and only if trA=0.

thm-span-of-commutators.title: Commutators Span the Trace-Zero Matrices
thm-span-of-commutators.html: Let F be any field and n≥1. The span of all commutators [X,Y] with X,Y∈Mn(F) is the subspace {A∈Mn(F):trA=0}. More precisely, every trace-zero matrix is a linear combination of the commutators Eij=[Eii,Eij] (i≠j)andEii−Enn=[Ein,Eni] (1≤i≤n−1).

thm-vec-identity.title: The vec Identity
thm-vec-identity.html: Let A∈Mk×m(F), X∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×l(F). Then vec(AXB)=(BT⊗A)vecX.

thm-woodbury.title: Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury Formula
thm-woodbury.html:
Let n,k≥1, let A∈Mn(F) and C∈Mk(F) be invertible, and let U∈Mn×k(F) and V∈Mk×n(F). Put W=C−1+VA−1U∈Mk(F).

  1. A+UCV is invertible if and only if W is invertible.
  2. In that case (A+UCV)−1=A−1−A−1UW−1VA−1=A−1−A−1U(C−1+VA−1U)−1VA−1.
  3. det(A+UCV)=detA⋅detC⋅detW.
